title: De signis Odysseae
author: Aristonicus of Alexandria

passages.original: Homerus non novit vocabulum νόμος, quod primum legitur in hymno ad Apollinem Delium v. 20. Itaque ad , ubi εὐνομίην legitur, ab εὖ νέμεσθαι derivatum esse Aristarchus docuit, cf. , certe ut Zenodoti lectionem refutaret, prae egregio νόον malam illam et falsam etiamsi decies νόμος apud Homerum legeretur. L. Ar. 348. Ad illum locum ab Aristonico citatum addi possunt etiam . Ceterum et Prellerus (ad ) et Sengebuschius () erraverunt in cod. Hamburgensi T. pro νόμον Zenodoti νόον legentes, haud dubie quod Ven.
passages.english: Homer did not know the word νόμος [law], which is first read in the Hymn to Delian Apollo, line 20. Therefore at [...], where εὐνομίην [good order] is read, Aristarchus taught that it was derived from εὖ νέμεσθαι [to be well distributed], cf. [...], certainly in order to refute Zenodotus' reading, [which preferred] in place of the excellent νόον [mind] that bad and false [reading], even if νόμος were read ten times in Homer. L. Ar. 348. To that passage cited by Aristonicus can also be added [...]. Moreover both Preller (on [...]) and Sengebusch ([...]) erred in reading in the Hamburg codex T. νόον for Zenodotus' νόμον, doubtless because [they did] not inspect Ven.
passages.notes: Several line references have dropped out of the scanned text (empty references after 'ad', 'cf.', 'Prellerus (ad )', etc.), marked [...]. The sentence 'certe ut Zenodoti lectionem refutaret, prae egregio νόον malam illam et falsam...' is elliptical and probably defective; the sense given is conjectural. The final sentence continues into the following context ('M. non inspexerunt'), i.e. 'Ven. M.'; the verb has been supplied from there.

passages.original: B et E conservaverunt Aristarchi observationem, duplicem Ephyram esse apud Homerum, unam Thesprotiae, alteram Corinthum cf. Sed non consentiunt, utram poeta nostro loco nominaverit. Recentiores interpretantur Thesprotiae urbem cf.
passages.english: [Scholia] B and E have preserved Aristarchus' observation that there are two Ephyras in Homer, one in Thesprotia, the other Corinth, cf. [...]. But they do not agree as to which of the two the poet named in our passage. More recent interpreters take it as the city of Thesprotia, cf. [...].
passages.notes: References after 'cf.' are missing in the scan.

passages.original: †) ἀνατολικοί. δεξιὰ γὰρ τὰ ἀνατολικὰ λέγει ὁ Ὅμηρος. εἴτ’ ἐπιδέξι’ ἴωσι πρὸς ἠώ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε, εἴτ’ ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ ποτὶ ζόφον ἠερόεντα. (). EQS.
passages.english: †) Eastern. For Homer calls the eastern [quarters] 'right': "whether they go to the right, toward the dawn and the sun, or to the left, toward the murky gloom" ([...]). EQS.
passages.notes: Line reference missing in the scan. 'EQS' are manuscript sigla.

passages.original: †) ὁ Ἀρίσταρχος λείπειν φησὶ τὸ ἄρθρον, ἵν’ ᾖ εἵνεκα τῆς ταύτης ἀρετῆς. Ἰακὸν δὲ τὸ ἔθος εἶναι. Ἀριστοφάνης δὲ ὑπώπτευε τὸν στίχον, νεωτερικὸν λέγων ὄνομα τὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς. HMQR — verba ὁ Ἀριστοφάνης — ἀρετῆς habet etiamS. — πιθανὸν δὲ συναθετεῖν αὐτῷ καὶ τὸν πρὸ αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸν μετ’ αὐτόν.
passages.english: †) Aristarchus says the article is missing, so that [the sense] is 'for the sake of this woman's excellence'; and that the usage is Ionic. But Aristophanes suspected the line, calling the word ἀρετή [excellence] a later one. HMQR — S also has the words 'Aristophanes — ἀρετῆς'. — It is plausible to athetize along with it both the line before it and the line after it.

passages.original: *) (ὁ στίχος οὗτος) ἀθετεῖται ὡς περιττός. προηθετεῖτο δὲ καὶ παρ’ Ἀριστοφάνει. (cod. προηθέτει δὲ καὶ Ἀριστοφάνης (MQR.
passages.english: *) (This line) is athetized as superfluous. It had also been athetized earlier by Aristophanes. (The codex [reads] 'Aristophanes too had athetized it earlier' (MQR.
passages.notes: Parenthesis left unclosed in the edition.

passages.original: οὐδὲ γὰρ νῦν οἱ περὶ Τηλέμαχον λῃστρικόν τι ἐμφαίνουσι. δοτέον δὲ, φησὶ, τῷ ποιητῇ τὰ τοιαῦτα. καὶ γὰρ ναῦν αὐτὸν παράγει εἰδότα, ἀλλά μοι εἴφ’ ὅπη ἔσχες ἰὼν εὐεργέα νῆα (), καὶ συνίησιν Ἑλληνίδα φωνήν. καθάπτεται δὲ καὶ Θουκυδίδου Ἀρίσταρχος λέγοντος ὡς οὐκ αἰσχρὸν ἡγοῦντο τὸ ληΐζεσθαι οἱ παλαιοὶ, ἐν οἷς φησιν οὕς μοι ληΐσσατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς (). ὁμωνυμίᾳ γὰρ ἠπάτηται, πολλάκις τῆς λῃΐδος ἐπὶ τῆς λαφυραγωγίας τασσομένης· παρὸ καὶ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν ληΐτιδα προσαγορεύει ().
passages.english: For not even now do Telemachus and his companions show anything piratical. But one must grant such things to the poet, he says. For he also presents him [the Cyclops] as knowing about a ship, 'but tell me where you put in, as you came, your well-built ship' ([...]), and as understanding the Greek language. Aristarchus also attacks Thucydides, who says that the ancients did not consider plundering shameful, in the passage where [Homer] says 'whom godlike Odysseus carried off as plunder for me' ([...]). For he has been deceived by the ambiguity of the word, since ληΐς [booty] is often used of the taking of spoils; which is why he also calls Athena ληΐτις [bringer of booty] ([...]).
passages.notes: Line references missing in the scan.

passages.original: cf. F. Ar. 30. γ 362. η 159. †) ὧδε: ἀεὶ παρὰ τῷ Ὁμήρῳ τὸ ὧδε ἀντὶ τοῦ κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον. BT.
passages.english: cf. F. Ar. 30. γ 362. η 159. †) ὧδε: in Homer ὧδε always stands for 'in this manner'. BT.

passages.original: †) καὶ παρὰ Ἀριστοφάνει προηθετοῦντο οὗτοι οἱ δύο στίχοι· ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ λόγου τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς (α 301) μετήχθησαν ἐνθάδε. HMQ. (μετηνέχθησαν Cobetus). καὶ addidit Dind. ex M. Aristonici verba sic fere restituenda sunt: ἀθετοῦνται οὗτοι οἱ δύο στίχοι μετὰ ἀστερίσκων ὅτι οὐ δεόντως ἐκ τοῦ λόγου τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς μετάκεινται ἐνθάδε.
passages.english: †) These two lines too had been athetized earlier by Aristophanes; for they were transferred here from Athena's speech (α 301). HMQ. (μετηνέχθησαν Cobet). Dindorf added καί from M. Aristonicus' words are to be restored roughly thus: 'These two lines are athetized with asterisks, because they have been transferred here improperly from Athena's speech.'

passages.original: Pertinet ad id, quod saepius Ar. adnotavit, nonnulla substantiva nunc in singulari, nunc in forma plurali apud Homerum legi. cf. L. Ar. 236. δ 514. η 80. θ 16. ι 80. ξ 199. ο 296. Eust. 1468, 12.
passages.english: This relates to what Aristarchus often noted, that some nouns are read in Homer now in the singular, now in the plural form. cf. L. Ar. 236. δ 514. η 80. θ 16. ι 80. ξ 199. ο 296. Eustathius 1468, 12.

passages.original: Notata fuit Zenodoti lectio δάμνιον pro ἄμνιον, ἅπαξ εἰρημένον cf. M.: ἄμνιον ἀγγεῖον εἰς ὅ τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἱερείου ἐδέχοντο. Ζηνόδοτος δὲ ἐν ταῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ δ γλώσσαις τίθησι τὴν λέξιν. ἅπαξ δὲ ἐνταῦθα παρ’ Ὁμήρῳ ἡ λέξιςM. cf.
passages.english: Zenodotus' reading δάμνιον for ἄμνιον, a word occurring only once, was noted; cf. M.: 'ἄμνιον: a vessel into which they received the blood of the sacrificial victim. Zenodotus places the word among his glosses from book δ. The word occurs only here in Homer.' M. cf. [...]
passages.notes: Final reference missing in the scan.

passages.original: *) [ἡ διπλῆ ὅτι] πάντα τὰ διατεταμένα νεῦρα τένοντας καλεῖ ὁ Ὅμηρος. EQM.cf. ad
passages.english: [The diple is there because] Homer calls all stretched sinews *tenontes* ("tendons"). EQM. Compare on
passages.notes: The cross-reference after "cf. ad" is cut off in the text. EQM are manuscript sigla.

passages.original: †) ὥσπερ ἀλλαχοῦ φησιν Ὅμηρος τάφον τὴν ἐπὶ τεθνεῶτί τινι εὐωχίαν, οὕτω καὶ νῦν γάμον τὴν ἐπὶ γάμου δαῖτα M.
passages.english: Just as elsewhere Homer calls the feast held over someone who has died *taphos* ("funeral"), so here too he calls the banquet at a wedding *gamos* ("wedding"). M.
passages.notes: M is a manuscript siglum.

passages.original: cf. Observatio est recta, apud Homerum vocabulum δοῦλον nusquam, δούλην uno modo loco reperiri pro δμὼς, δμωή. At v. 396-418 expunxit Aristarchus. Aristonicus quidem alias caussas enumerat, sed facile in tam multis excidere poterat illa, quod in novo vocabulo δούλη haesitabat, et verisimile est, ut Friedlaenderus monet, hoc suspicionem auxisse.
passages.english: Compare. The observation is correct: in Homer the word *doulos* ("slave") is found nowhere, and *doulē* ("slave-woman") in only one place, instead of *dmōs*, *dmōē*. But Aristarchus expunged lines 396–418. Aristonicus, it is true, lists other reasons, but among so many that one could easily have dropped out, namely that [Aristarchus] hesitated over the new word *doulē*. And it is likely, as Friedlaender points out, that this increased the suspicion.
passages.notes: The passage is a Latin editorial note, although it is labelled grc.

passages.original: †) προηθετοῦντο καὶ παρὰ Ζηνοδότῳ καὶ παρὰ Ἀριστοφάνει· τό τε γὰρ σφῶϊν οὐχ Ὁμηρικῶς μονοσυλλάβως ἐξηνέχθη ὅ τε ἔπαινος τῶν νέων οὐκ ἀναγκαῖος HM.
passages.english: They were athetised already by Zenodotus and by Aristophanes. For *sphōin* was uttered as a monosyllable, which is not Homeric, and the praise of the young men is not necessary. HM.

passages.original: Diple fuit contra chorizontes, qui opponebant, solum in Odyssea heroes piscibus vesci, non in Iliade. Contra hos Aristarchus recte demonstravit, quaedam heroibus cognita quidem fuisse, quibus Homerus heroas utentes non faciat. Fortasse hoc etiam Ar. obtendit, quod Homerus ipse dicit: ἔτειρε δὲ γαστέρα λιμός et schol. in B affert: ἀλλαχόσε οὐ λέγει ὁ Ὅμηρος ἐσθίειν τοὺς Ἕλληνας (l. ἥρωας) ἰχθύας· νῦν δέ φησι τούτους ἀγρεύειν ἰχθύας διὰ τὸ τείρεσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ λιμοῦ. cf. ad
passages.english: The diple was [aimed] against the Separatists, who objected that only in the Odyssey, and not in the Iliad, do the heroes eat fish. Against them Aristarchus rightly showed that certain things were indeed known to the heroes which Homer does not make the heroes use. Perhaps Aristarchus also pointed to what Homer himself says: "and hunger wore at their bellies". And the scholion in B adds: "Elsewhere Homer does not say that the Greeks (read: heroes) eat fish, but here he says that they catch fish because they are worn down by hunger." Compare on
passages.notes: Latin editorial note with embedded Greek. The cross-reference at the end is cut off. "Chorizontes" were those who assigned the Iliad and Odyssey to different authors.

passages.original: *) ὅτι τὸν Νεῖλον Αἴγυπτον ὀνομάζει, ὁ δὲ Ἡσίοδος ὡς ὢν νεώτερος Νεῖλον αὐτὸν οἶδεν ἤδη καλούμενον. HMPQT.
passages.english: [The sign is there] because he calls the Nile *Aigyptos*, whereas Hesiod, being later, knows it as already called the Nile. HMPQT.

passages.original: cf. Alii: Τροίης ἀπὸ ληίδος. Fluxisse videtur ex Ar., qui observavit, Troiam urbem apud Homerum δισυλλάβως legi Τροίην, adiectivum contra Τροΐην τρισυλλάβως de urbe aliqua Troiana.
passages.english: Compare. Others [read]: *Troiēs apo lēidos* ("from the Trojan booty"). This seems to derive from Aristarchus, who observed that in Homer the city of Troy is read with two syllables as *Troiēn*, whereas the adjective *Troïēn*, with three syllables, refers to some Trojan city.
passages.notes: Latin editorial note.

passages.original: Pieriam enim, Olympi cacumen, transcendunt dii apud Homerum, iter facientes ex Olympo in terram.
passages.english: For in Homer the gods pass over Pieria, a summit of Olympus, when they travel from Olympus to the earth.
passages.notes: Latin editorial note.

passages.original: Adnotare solebat Ar. haec epitheta apud Homerum nominibus quasi propria et ita firmiter adhaerentia, ut ne tum quidem divelli possint, si significatio eorum ab aliquo loco vel tempore aliena sit. cf. et exempla ibid.
passages.english: Aristarchus used to note that in Homer these epithets cling to names as though they were proper to them, and so firmly that they cannot be torn away even when their meaning is foreign to a particular place or time. Compare also the examples in the same place.
passages.notes: Latin editorial note.

passages.original: *) ἀθετεῖται τὸ ἔπος ὡς ἀσύμφωνον τῇ τοῦ Ὁμήρου συνηθείᾳ. οὐ γὰρ ποιεῖ τὰς τραπέζας ἀφαιρουμένας παρόντων τῶν δαιτυμόνων, ἀλλὰ μετὰ τὴν ἀπαλλαγήν. HPQT.
passages.english: The line is athetised as inconsistent with Homer's usage. For he does not make the tables be removed while the diners are present, but after they have departed. HPQT.

passages.original: Fluxit ex Ar. qui ad posuit diplam, ὅτι δύο διαστάσεις οἶδεν Ὅμηρος κοσμικὰς ἀνατολὴν καὶ δύσιν. cf.
passages.english: It derives from Aristarchus, who placed a diple [at the line], [noting] that Homer knows two cosmic regions, east and west. Compare.
passages.notes: Latin commentary with Greek quotation; line references and the cross-reference after 'cf.' are missing from the text as held. 'ad posuit' read as 'apposuit'.

passages.original: Certe adnotatum fuit, vocabulum ἦ poni tantum post orationem peractam, vid. schol. in E, quod legitur etiam ad et Porphyrii est, qui idem docuit atque Aristarchus, sed plures exquirit vocabulorum ἦ et φῆ differentias. cf.
passages.english: It was certainly noted that the word ē ('he spoke') is placed only after a speech has been completed; see the scholion on E, which is also read at [...], and which belongs to Porphyry, who taught the same as Aristarchus but investigates further differences between the words ē and phē. Compare.
passages.notes: Verse references after 'ad' and 'cf.' are missing in the text as held.

passages.original: Demodoci cantum de Martis cum Venere amoribus in offensionem veterum grammaticorum incurrisse constat ex schol. ad : σημειοῦται ταῦτα ὁ Μόχθος (i. e. Apio, quem hoc cognomine appellatum esse prodidit Suidas) πρὸς τοὺς ἀθετοῦντας τὴν ἐν Ὀδυσσείᾳ Ἄρεως καὶ Ἀφροδίτης μοιχείαν. Scholiasta in HQT dicit: ἀλλ’ οὐχ Ὁμήρου τὸ ἔγκλημα. Quo magis dolemus, quod quid Ar. hac de re statuerit nobis non servatum est. Hoc unum ex scholiis ad Iliadem extricamus, Aristarchum non haesitasse ut chorizontes, quod nostro loco Venus Vulcani uxor est, cf.
passages.english: That Demodocus' song about the loves of Mars and Venus gave offence to the ancient grammarians is clear from the scholion on [...]: "Mochthos (that is, Apion, who Suidas reports was called by this nickname) marks these lines against those who athetize the adultery of Ares and Aphrodite in the Odyssey." The scholiast in HQT says: "But the charge is not Homer's." All the more do we regret that what Aristarchus decided on this matter has not been preserved for us. This one thing we extract from the scholia on the Iliad: that Aristarchus did not hesitate, as the chorizontes [the 'separators', who denied that the two poems had the same author] did, over the fact that in our passage Venus is Vulcan's wife; compare
passages.notes: Line references missing after 'ad'. 'Mochthos' ('Toil') as Apion's nickname is as the text gives it.

passages.original: †) Ἡσίοδος ἐκ μόνης τῆς Ἥρας γενέσθαι τὸν Ἥφαιστον. κἀκεῖνο δ’ ἱκανὸν τόν τοι φίλος υἱὸς ἔτευξεν Ἥφαιστος (). T. sc. ut Hesiodus refutetur, nam Jovis et Junonis filius est apud Homerum cf. ad ubi noster locus citatur.
passages.english: †) Hesiod [says] that Hephaestus was born of Hera alone. And this too is sufficient [against him]: "which your dear son Hephaestus made" (). That is, so that Hesiod may be refuted, for in Homer he is the son of Jupiter and Juno; compare the note at [...] where our passage is cited.
passages.notes: The second part is a Latin editorial note, translated as such. Line references are missing from the text (empty parentheses, and a blank after "ad").

passages.original: †) ταῦτα σημειοῦνταί τινες πρὸς τὸ μὴ παραδιδόναι Ὅμηρον Διόνυσον οἴνου εὑρέτην, τὸν δὲ Μάρωνα οὐ Διονύσου, ἀλλ’ Ἀπόλλωνος ἱερέα, δι’ ὅλης τῆς ποιήσεως οἴνου μνημονεύων· ἡ δ’ ἀπότασις πρὸς Ἡσίοδον λέγοντα τὸν Μάρωνα εἶναι Οἰνοπίωνος τοῦ Διονύσου HQ.
passages.english: †) Some mark these lines [to show] that Homer does not hand down Dionysus as the discoverer of wine, and [makes] Maron a priest not of Dionysus but of Apollo, although he mentions wine throughout the whole poem; the polemic is directed against Hesiod, who says that Maron was [the son] of Oenopion, son of Dionysus. HQ.
passages.notes: 'apotasis' taken in the sense of 'reference/target of the note'.

passages.original: Ad Ar. adnotavit, verbum θύειν nusquam apud Homerum dici de immolanda hostia sed de offerendis ἀπαρχαί, et θυηλάς esse ἀπαρχάς cf. Hoc certe ad nostrum etiam versum observatum fuit contra Philoxenum, qui falso accepit τὸ ἔνθα δὲ πῦρ κήαντες ἐθύσαμενπαρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ εἴρησθαι ἐπὶ τῶν ἀρνῶν.
passages.english: At [...] Aristarchus noted that the verb thyein is nowhere in Homer used of slaughtering a victim, but of offering first-fruits (aparchai), and that thyēlai are first-fruits; compare. This was certainly observed at our line too, against Philoxenus, who wrongly took the words 'there, having kindled a fire, we made offering' to be said by the poet of the lambs.
passages.notes: Line reference missing after 'Ad'. 'ἐθύσαμενπαρὰ' read as two words.

passages.original: †) ὁ (δὲ) Ἀρίσταρχος πλωτῇ ἀντὶ τοῦ φορητῇ, οἷον περιφερομένη, ὡς ποτὲ μὲν ἐν τοῖς δεξιοῖς μέρεσι, ποτὲ δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἀριστεροῖς ὁρᾶσθαι, οἷον δή τι καὶ περὶ τὴν Δῆλον ἱστορεῖ Πίνδαρος λέγων οὕτως ἦν γὰρ τὸ πάροιθε φορητὰ κυμάτεσσι Δᾶλος παντοδαπῶν τ’ ἀνέμων ῥιπαῖς () HMQTV. Qpraeterea habet: οἰκειότερον γάρ φησι μὴ ἐῤῥιζῶσθαι τῶν ἀνέμων νῆσον. Eust. idem. cf.
passages.english: †) Aristarchus [takes] plōtē ('floating') in place of phorētē ('carried about'), that is, moving around, so that it is seen sometimes on the right side, sometimes on the left; just such a thing Pindar also relates about Delos, saying thus: 'For formerly Delos was carried by the waves and by the blasts of winds of every kind' (...). HMQTV. Q has in addition: 'For he says it is more fitting that the island of the winds should not be rooted.' Eustathius [says] the same. Compare.
passages.notes: 'Qpraeterea' read as 'Q praeterea'. Pindar reference missing.

passages.original: Versum 189 Callistratus a grammatico quodam, qui nullam illius Homeri consuetudinis ἀπὸ τοῦ γὰρ ἄρχεσθαι cognitionem habuerit, insertum esse dicit cf. in H. Καλλίστρατός φησιν ὡς ὑπό τινος ὁ στίχος προτέτακται ἀγνοοῦντος τὸ Ὁμηρικὸν ἔθος, ὡς θέλει ἄρχεσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ γάρ. Aristarchus versum non legisse videtur, nam diplam posuit propter hunc Homeri usum et citavit ob eandem causam.
passages.english: Callistratus says that line 189 was inserted by some grammarian who had no knowledge of that habit of Homer's of beginning with 'for' (gar); compare in H: "Callistratus says that the line was prefixed by someone ignorant of the Homeric custom, that he likes to begin with 'for'." Aristarchus seems not to have read the line, for he placed a diple on account of this usage of Homer and cited [it] for the same reason.

passages.original: Refutatio fuit Cratetis, qui quatuor coeli regiones Homero notas fuisse ex hoc loco contendit. Aristarchus recte eum duas modo orientem et occasum novisse docuit. cf. ἠὼς σημαίνει καὶ τὴν ἡλίου πάροδον, καὶ τὸν τόπον ὅθεν ἀνατέλλει ὁ ἥλιος κατὰ Ἀρίσταρχον· Sequuntur vs. 190-92. νῦν γὰρ, καθά φησιν ὁ Κράτης, τῶν τεσσάρων τοῦ κόσμου μέμνηται μερῶν, ἄρκτου, μεσημβρίας, ἀνατολῆς καὶ δύσεως κ.
passages.english: It was a refutation of Crates, who argued from this passage that the four regions of the sky were known to Homer. Aristarchus rightly showed that he knew only two, east and west. Compare: "Ēōs signifies both the sun's passage and the place from which the sun rises, according to Aristarchus." Lines 190–92 follow. "For here, as Crates says, he mentions the four parts of the world, north, south, east and west," etc.

passages.original: *) ὅτι κουρίδιον αὐτόν φησιν. ἔνιοι γὰρ γεγαμῆσθαι τὴν Κλυταιμνήστραν Ταντάλῳ, ὡς Εὐριπίδης () εἰςάγει αὐτὴν λέγουσαν ἔγημας ἄκουσάν με κἄλαβες βίᾳ τὸν πρόσθεν ἄνδρα Τάνταλον κατακτανώνQ. cf.
passages.english: *) [The sign is] because he calls him her wedded husband (kouridios). For some [say] that Clytemnestra had been married to Tantalus, as Euripides (...) brings her on saying: 'You married me against my will and took me by force, having killed my former husband Tantalus.' Q. Compare.
passages.notes: Euripides reference missing.

passages.original: *) ὅτι αὐτοὺς τὰ σώματα αὐτῶν φησιν Ὅμηρος, οὐκ ἂν δέοι σώματος ἐν θεοῖςH. cf. ad In cod. G v. 602-4 obelis notati sunt et in legitur ad v. 602-3: οὗτοι ἀθετοῦνται καὶ λέγονται Ὀνομακρίτου εἶναι. cf. Ad v. 604 H habet: τοῦτο ὑπὸ Ὀνομακρίτου ἐμπεποιῆσθαί φασιν.
passages.english: *) [The sign is] because Homer calls their bodies 'themselves'; there would be no need of a body among the gods. H. Compare at [...]. In codex G lines 602–4 are marked with obeli, and in [...] at lines 602–3 it reads: "These are athetized and are said to be by Onomacritus." Compare. At line 604 H has: "They say this was interpolated by Onomacritus."
passages.notes: Opening scholion is elliptical; sense uncertain. Some references missing.

passages.original: ἔνιοι δὲ βιαιότερον ὑπερβάτως κολλῶντες τὸ Ὠκεανοῖο τῷ ὅθι τ’ ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης, οὗ, φασὶν, οἰκεῖ ἡ ἡμέρα· ἐξ αὐτοῦ γὰρ ἀνατέλλει καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν δύνει. οὐ μόνον δέ ἐστι βίαιον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐναντίον τῷ ποιητῇ· οὐ γὰρ παραδίδωσιν ὁ Ὅμηρος τοὺς ήρωας ἐπισταμένους ὅτι ἐξ Ὠκεανοῦ αἱ ἀνατολαὶ τοῦ ἡλίου, ἀλλ’ αὐτὸς ἐκ τοῦ ἰδίου προσώπου τὸ τοιοῦτον παρέδωκεν. ἠέλιος μὲν ἔπειτα νέον προσέβαλλεν ἀρούρας ἐξ ἀκαλαῤῥείταο βαθυῤῥόου Ὠκεανοῖο ()· καὶ ἐν δ’ ἔπεσ’ Ὠκεανῷ φάος ἠελίοιο (). οἱ δὲ ἥρωες ἄλλως λέγουσιν. οὐδ’ ὅπη ἠέλιος φαεσίμβροτος εἶσ’ ὑπὸ γαῖαν () Q.
passages.english: Some, more forcibly, join "of Ocean" by hyperbaton to "where [are the dwellings] of early-born Dawn", [meaning], they say, where the day dwells; for it rises out of it and sets into it. But this is not only forced, it is also contrary to the poet; for Homer does not present the heroes as knowing that the risings of the sun are from Ocean, but he himself, in his own person, gave out such a thing: "The sun then was newly striking the fields, out of gently flowing, deep-streaming Ocean"; and "the light of the sun fell into Ocean." But the heroes speak otherwise: "nor where the sun that brings light to mortals goes beneath the earth" Q.
passages.notes: Scholiastic note with manuscript siglum (Q); verse references are missing in the edition (empty parentheses). 'ήρωας' read as 'ἥρωας'.

passages.original: †) κατὰ Ὅμηρον δύο· Σειρήνοιν γὰρ λέγει V. Ὅμηρος οὔτε γένος αὐτῶν παρίστησιν οὔτε πτερωτὰς αὐτάς φησιν εἶναι HQT. cf.
passages.english: †) According to Homer [the Sirens are] two; for he says "of the two Sirens" (Seirēnoin, dual) V. Homer neither sets out their parentage nor says that they are winged HQT. Cf.
passages.notes: Letters V, HQT are manuscript sigla. The cross-reference after 'cf.' is missing.

passages.original: †) ὁ μὲν Ἀριστοφάνης φησὶ κατατηκομένους τῇ ᾠδῇ καὶ αἰφνιδίως ἐκλείποντας ἀπολέσθαι, ὅ δὲ Ἀρίσταρχος διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀναγκαίων σπάνιν Q. [ἥν πάσχουσι προστετηκότες ἐπὶ μακρὸν τῇ ᾠδῇ]. ex addidi.
passages.english: †) Aristophanes says that they perished wasting away through the song and suddenly failing, but Aristarchus [says it was] through lack of necessities Q. [which they suffer, having long clung fast to the song]. I have added [this] from [...].
passages.notes: The bracketed clause is an editorial supplement; the source after 'ex' is missing in the text. Q is a manuscript siglum.

passages.original: *) ὅτι δύο καθ’ Ὅμηρον αἱ Σειρῆνες, οὐ τρεῖςQ. cf. ad
passages.english: *) [The sign is] because according to Homer the Sirens are two, not three Q. Cf. on [...]
passages.notes: Cross-reference missing; 'τρεῖςQ' read as 'τρεῖς Q'.

passages.original: Notatus fuit versus propter metrum initii, cf. ad: τὰ γὰρ τοιαῦτα ἐσημειοῦντο πρὸς κρίσιν ποιημάτων, ὅτι σπανίως Ὅμηρος κακομέτρους ποιεῖ.
passages.english: The line was marked on account of the metre of its beginning, cf. on [...]: for they used to mark such things for the judging of poems, since Homer rarely makes faulty lines.
passages.notes: Mixed Latin editorial note and Greek scholium; cross-reference missing.

passages.original: *) ὅτι οἱ ἑστιώμενοι παρ’ Ὁμήρῳ τοῖς ἑστιῶσι προπίνουσιν, ὡς Ὀδυσσεὺς Ἀχιλλεῖ καὶ Εὐμαίῳ ὁ αὐτὸς H. cf. ad
passages.english: *) [The sign is] because those being feasted in Homer drink a toast to their hosts, as Odysseus [does] to Achilles, and the same [Odysseus] to Eumaeus H. Cf. on [...]
passages.notes: Cross-reference missing; H is a manuscript siglum.

passages.original: nam sic Aristarchum interpretatum esse ut B. cod. docet : διὰ δὲ τοῦ Ἀριστάρχου ὑπομνήματος ἰονθάδος ἔνιοι ἀποδιδόασι τελείου. εἴη δ’ ἂν λεγόμενον ἀπὸ τῶν ἰόνθων. τὰς γὰρ τῶν τριχῶν ῥίζας ἰόνθους λέγει Σοφοκλῆς ἐν Χρύσῃἐγὼ μέλαιναν ἐξιονθίζω τρίχα (corr. Lehrsius pro μίαν μέν cod.). Huc referendum est, quod legitur in H ad : οὐκ ἂν νῦν ἔφη δασύ, εἴ γε τὸ ἰονθάδος ἐδήλου τὸ δασέος (ut voluit Apion cf. ).
passages.english: For that Aristarchus interpreted it so is shown by codex B: "But through Aristarchus' commentary some render ionthados as 'full-grown'. It would be said from the ionthoi; for Sophocles in the Chryses calls the roots of the hair ionthoi: 'I pluck out my black hair'" (corrected by Lehrs for μίαν μέν of the codex). To this must be referred what is read in H on [...]: "He would not now have said 'shaggy', if indeed ionthados meant 'shaggy'" (as Apion wished, cf. [...]).
passages.notes: Mixed Latin editorial and Greek. 'ἐν Χρύσῃἐγὼ' read as 'ἐν Χρύσῃ· ἐγὼ'. References missing in places.

passages.original: †) ἀτόπως καὶ τὸ ἀν’ Ἑλλάδα. μόνην γὰρ τὴν ὑπὸ Ἀχιλλεῖ Ἑλλάδα καλεῖ Ὅμηρος Q. cf. ad
passages.english: †) "Throughout Hellas" is also out of place; for Homer calls only the [region] under Achilles Hellas Q. Cf. on [...]
passages.notes: Cross-reference missing.

passages.original: Versum 91 ἤ τί μοι ἐκ μεγάρων κειμήλιον ἐσθλὸν ὄληται Aristophanes propter eandem caussam ut v. 19 expunxisse videtur, cf. schol. in H. ἔστι σμικρολόγου ὡς Ἀριστοφάνης φησί.
passages.english: Line 91, "or some fine treasure of mine from the halls is lost", Aristophanes seems to have deleted for the same reason as line 19; cf. the scholium in H: "It is [the line] of a petty-minded man, as Aristophanes says."

passages.original: †) Ἄργεος οὐ τῆς πόλεως, ἀλλὰ τῆς χώραςB. Fluxit ex Ar., qui apud Homerum Peloponnesum Argos nominari observavit, non urbem ut apud recentiores. cf.
passages.english: †) "Of Argos" not the city, but the country B. This derives from Aristarchus, who observed that in Homer the Peloponnese is called Argos, not the city as in later writers. Cf. [...]
passages.notes: 'Ar.' taken as Aristarchus; cross-reference missing.

passages.original: †) πρὸς τὴν δειλινὴν ὥραν παραγενόμενος, τουτέστι τὴν μεσημβρίαν· ἢ τὴν ἑσπερινὴν διατρίψας. ἔνιοι δὲ τὴν δειλινὴν τροφὴν αἰτῶν. καὶ Καλλίμαχός φησι δείελον αἰτίζουσιν, ἄγουσι δὲ χεῖρας ἀπ’ ἔργου, τὴν πρὸς τῇ δειλινῇ τροφὴν αἰτοῦντες. οὐ δεόντως. προειρήκαμεν γὰρ ὅτι οἱ ἀρχαῖοι τρισὶ τροφαῖς ἐχρῶντο V. Idem breviusBH: ἔνιοι τὴν δείλην διατρίψας, οὐ φαγών.
passages.english: †) Arriving toward the afternoon (*deilinē*) hour, that is, midday; or, having spent the evening. Some [take it as] asking for the afternoon meal. And Callimachus says, "they ask for the *deielos* [afternoon meal], and they draw their hands away from work," meaning those asking for the meal at afternoon. [This is] not correct, for we have said before that the ancients used three meals. V. The same more briefly, BH: some [take it as] "having spent the afternoon," not "having eaten."
passages.notes: The lemma being commented on is not given; the note concerns Homeric δείελος/δειελιήσας (Odyssey 17.599). V, BH, HQV etc. are manuscript sigla. The edition's cross-reference numbers are missing after "cf." here and in the following units.

passages.original: cf. ἔσσο legitur apud Homerum
passages.english: cf. *esso* ["be clothed"] is read in Homer.
passages.notes: Fragmentary editorial note, partly in Latin; the reference is missing.

passages.original: *) [ἡ διπλῆ ὅτι τὸ λύχνον] ἀπὸ τοῦ λύειν τὸ νύχος. λέγει δὲ τὴν δᾷδα κυρίως· τοῦ δὲ παρ’ ἡμῖν καλουμένου λύχνου τοὺς ἥρωας χρωμένους ὁ ποιητὴς οὐκ εἰςάγει. οὐδὲ Ἡσίοδος μέμνηται HQV. cf. ad: λύχνος ὁ λύων τὸ νύχος, τουτέστι τὸ σκότος. οὕτως Ἀριστόνικος ἐν τῷ περὶ σημείων τοῦ Ὁμήρου.
passages.english: *) [The diplē (marginal sign) is there because *lychnon* (lamp)] is from *lyein to nychos* ["loosing the night"]. It properly means the torch; the poet does not represent the heroes as using what we call a *lychnos* [oil lamp]. Nor does Hesiod mention it. HQV. cf. on: *lychnos* is that which loosens the *nychos*, that is, the darkness. So Aristonicus in his work On the Signs of Homer.
passages.notes: The bracketed opening is an editorial restoration. HQV are manuscript sigla; the cross-reference after "cf. ad" is missing.

passages.original: *) [ἀθετοῦνται οἱ στίχοι ὅτι] οὐδέποτε Ὅμηρος ἐπὶ τοῦ ἔλεγε τὸ ἴσκε, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τοῦ ὁμοίου· ἠπάτηται οὖν ὁ διασκευαστὴς ἐκ τοῦ ἴσκε ψεύδεα πολλὰ λέγων ἐτύμοισιν ὅμοια ().
passages.english: *) [The lines are athetized because] Homer never [uses] *iske* in the sense of "he said," but in the sense of "like"; so the reviser (*diaskeuastēs*) was misled by "he made (*iske*) many falsehoods like the truth."
passages.notes: The text appears defective: "ἐπὶ τοῦ ἔλεγε" lacks a verb such as τίθησι, supplied in sense. The quoted line is Odyssey 19.203; the empty parentheses mark a missing reference.

passages.original: †) σημειῶδες· ἀεὶ γὰρ τὸ βάλλειν παρ’, Ὁμήρῳ ἐπὶ τοῦ τυχεῖν H. cf.
passages.english: †) Noteworthy: for in Homer *ballein* [to throw] is always [used] of hitting [the target]. H. cf.
passages.notes: The cross-reference is missing.

passages.original: 1 †) Ἀρίσταρχος ἀθετεῖ τὴν νέκυιαν κεφαλαίοις τοῖς συνεκτικωτάτοις τοῖςδε. ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι καθ’ Ὅμηρον ψυχοπομπὸς ὁ Ἑρμῆς cf. ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ χθόνιος ὁ θεός. Κυλλήνιος δὲ οὐδαμοῦ εἴρηται εἰ μὴ (corr. Spohnius pro ἢ) ἅπαξ. ἀλλὰ πῶς αἱ ψυχαὶ οὐκ αὐτόμαται κατίασιν, ὡς ἐν Ἰλιάδι; (cf. ad), ἀλλ’ αὗται καὶ ἄταφοι κατίασιν (cf.
passages.english: 1 †) Aristarchus athetizes the *Nekyia* [the second underworld scene] on these most cogent main grounds: that in Homer Hermes is not a conductor of souls (cf.), nor is the god chthonic. And "Cyllenian" is nowhere said except (Spohn's correction for "or") once. But how is it that the souls do not go down of their own accord, as in the Iliad? (cf. on), but these go down even though unburied (cf.
passages.notes: Refers to the second Nekyia (Odyssey 24). The sentence breaks off mid-reference and continues in the following passage; the rhetorical question seems to be an objection to the scene.
